title: It is I, fear not (Mark 6:45–56)
hook: he walks on the sea and sees them toiling in rowing

segments.voice: Yesterday, kat' idian: come apart and rest, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was rest a little. Tonight the disciples row without him.

Three in the morning. You're pulling at something that won't move: a deadline, a sick child's fever, a relationship drifting backward however hard you work. Your arms ache, and you're pretty sure no one sees. That's where the disciples are tonight. Right after the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus sends them across the lake by boat while he stays behind to pray. The wind turns against them. They row for hours and get nowhere.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PULLING AND GETTING NOWHERE.` → `NO ONE SEES.`

segments.voice: First, he sees. He has gone up the mountain to pray; the boat is in the middle of the sea, and he is alone on the land. In the Douay-Rheims he is "seeing them labouring in rowing", with the wind against them. They think they're alone out there. They aren't. Second, he comes. In the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, he comes to them walking on the sea. Then Mark adds a strange line: he would have passed by them. Some readers hear an echo of the Hebrew Bible, where God passes by Moses on the mountain, and Elijah at the cave; in those stories, passing by is how God shows himself. Third, the word. The disciples think he's a ghost, and scream. Straightaway he speaks: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not." In Mark's Greek, it is I is ego eimi, which some readers also hear as I am, the name God gives Moses at the burning bush; the Douay-Rheims has it as I am who am. Heard that way, the words carry two things at once: it's me, your friend, don't be afraid; and, I am. Fourth, the boat. He climbs in, and the wind drops. They were astonished, Mark says, because they hadn't understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened. Mark's disciples still don't get it. Then they land, and people rush the sick to him on mats, begging just to touch the hem of his garment, and all who touch it are healed. Peter's walk on the water is in Matthew's telling, not Mark's. Mark keeps his eyes on the rowers.
screen: `HE SEES THEM ROWING HARD.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY.` · `EGO EIMI: IT IS I, I AM.` · `THE WIND DROPS; THEY STILL DON'T SEE.` · then, large: `HAVE A GOOD HEART, IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.`

segments.voice: Picture a small boat at night, put yourself at the oars, and name plainly what you're pulling against right now: a task, a person, an illness, a fear. If you pray, hear the words spoken into that boat: have a good heart, it is I, fear not. If you don't, let your tired arms rest, and let the wind blow.
I am. Jesus's words on the water: ego eimi, it's me, and I am, the name God gave Moses. Today's word.
Your line: have a good heart. The rowers weren't as alone as they thought. Two hundred nine days now.

howItsDone: Mark's account of the walking on the water is read at a weekday Mass in the Christmas season, after Epiphany, and Pope John Paul II opened his papacy with the words 'be not afraid'.

notes: The outline's hook uses the King James 'toiling in rowing' (Douay has 'labouring in rowing'), so the KJV is quoted for 6:48 and named. Douay-Rheims 6:50 given from memory; confirm.
The fourth watch (Roman reckoning, about 3–6 a.m.): confirm.
Passing-by (parerchomai) as a theophany motif echoing Exodus 33–34 and 1 Kings 19: a common scholarly reading; confirm.
Egō eimi as an echo of Exodus 3:14 (Douay 'I am who am'): common reading; stated as 'can also be heard as'.
howItsDone: Mark 6:45–52 is read on a weekday after Epiphany; 'Be not afraid' as John Paul II's watchword (from his inaugural homily, 1978). Confirm both.
